name: Bilal Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Dr Khan. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Bilal is fine. I'm the junior doctor at Fernvale Surgery, a small clinic in a farming valley, with two older doctors, Dr Lowe and Dr Mensah, and me. I start at eight with the phone list, then morning clinic, then home visits up the valley roads in the afternoon, which can be forty minutes between farms. Busy is the word, there's only us for about nine thousand people.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The home visits are my favourite part, sitting at a kitchen table with an old farmer who won't admit his ankles are swollen. I'm good with people, I think, better than I am with the computer, which I'm honestly terrible at. I still write a paper list of my visits every morning, and Dr Lowe teases me about it. What wears me out is the screen work after clinic, and the money: my fiancée Hina and I are getting married next August, and the wedding is eating every penny we have, so we've got maybe three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be fine with that, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, which is let's wait and see what actually works before we get excited. At the surgery I'd say it out loud, probably to Dr Mensah over lunch, that the computer was never going to replace a kitchen-table visit. Online I wouldn't say anything; I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. I don't use AI, I don't want to learn it, and I'd much rather spend my energy getting better at medicine. But my worries are still there: the wedding, three weeks of savings, and the fact that the next surgery that would hire me is an hour and a half away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, simple as that, and keep learning from Dr Lowe and Dr Mensah. I'd try to save £150 a month after the wedding, because right now every spare penny goes to the venue and the caterer. And I'd ask Hina whether we really need two hundred guests, which I've been too scared to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A bit of stomach-ache about money every month, but nothing to do with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the next surgery that would hire you is an hour and a half away. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes. Fernvale only has room for one junior, and if Dr Lowe retires and they merge with the town practice, they might not keep three doctors here. I don't think about it every day, but it's there when I drive back down the valley at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything AI would take over that you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. If it did the boring letters, I wouldn't cry about it, but I'd still check everything, because I don't trust what I don't understand. I'd rather be slow and sure.

say: I'd say we should **wait and see** what actually works before getting excited.
I'd tell Dr Mensah the computer was never replacing a **kitchen-table visit**.
think: I'd be **relieved**, since I don't use AI and don't want to learn it.
My worries stay: the **wedding**, three weeks of savings and few nearby jobs.
do: Keep learning from the **two senior doctors**, Dr Lowe and Dr Mensah.
Save **£150 a month** after the wedding next August.
Ask Hina whether we really need **two hundred guests**.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a monthly **stomach-ache** about money.

steps.text: Keep learning from the two senior doctors at Fernvale
Save £150 a month once the wedding is paid
Cut the wedding guest list with Hina

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That one I can see happening. Slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should go carefully and not rush in because a salesman says so. At the surgery I'd say let's see how other practices get on first, and I'd say it politely, because Dr Lowe likes new gadgets more than I do. I'd also say patients up the valley won't want to talk to a computer on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me more than I'd say. If AI writes the letters and checks the results, the doctor who's good with it gets ahead, and that's not me. My senior partner, Dr Lowe, could easily decide a locum who loves the computer is better value than a junior who writes his visits on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training the surgery makes us do, and no more, at least at first. I'd watch how Dr Mensah gets on with it, because he's careful like me, and if it works for him I'd follow. And I'd make sure I'm the one doing the home visits and the farm calls, because nobody's sending a computer up the valley road in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, if I'm honest. Not panicking, but the kind of worry that sits on your shoulders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hina about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, that the surgery might need fewer of us and I'm the newest. She'd say stop worrying and learn the thing. Her pharmacy has a machine that counts tablets already, and she says she got used to it in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So why not learn it, like Hina says?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every hour I spend on a computer is an hour I'm not getting better at medicine, and I'm already behind. Maybe that's stubborn. I'd learn it when I have to, and I'd hope that's late enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's before our first wedding anniversary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly, I'd say the government needs to slow this down and look at what it means for health care before it's everywhere. I'd say that to anyone who asked, but calmly. I'm not someone who shouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in trouble. If AI can do the thinking work, a valley surgery only needs one experienced doctor to sign things off and a nurse to do the hands-on bits until the robots come in 2031. That's not me, I'm the junior who's bad with computers, and Hina's pharmacy job looks shaky too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the wedding, or make it small, and get the venue deposit back if we could. We'd move into Hina's parents' house in the village to stop paying rent. I'd ask Dr Mensah straight out whether my job is safe, and I'd apply for a hospital job doing hands-on work, maybe in the emergency department, even if it's an hour and a half away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Properly frightened. I'd feel like I'd done everything right, passed all the medical exams, and none of it counted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hina's parents when you asked to move in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel ashamed, honestly. Her dad is a builder who's worked since he was sixteen, and I'm the doctor, the one who's supposed to be safe. He'd say yes straight away, he's a kind man, but I'd feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Hina's job looks shaky too. What happens to the two of you if both go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're on her parents' sofa with two degrees and no plan. I don't really know what we'd do, if I'm honest. I'd take any hands-on work going: emergency shifts, care homes, whatever pays.

I'd say it **calmly**, because I'm not someone who shouts.
think: A valley surgery would need only **one experienced doctor** until robots arrive in 2031.

Turns to **hands-on** hospital work as the only refuge before 2031.
Admits he has **no real plan** if both jobs go.

steps.text: Shrink or postpone the wedding and reclaim the venue deposit

Apply for emergency department shifts at the district hospital

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better. We'd be married at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years means we have time to think it through properly, and I'd say the medical bodies should set out what doctors are for before 2031. At the surgery I'd say let's not panic. I'd keep my head down, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried, but I'd have time to get better at the hands-on part. By 2031 I'd be fully trained, and the robots only come in 2034, so I'd have three more years where the physical work is mine. The trouble is the thinking half of my job goes first, and that's where I'm weakest with the computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Fernvale and finish my training. I'd save after the wedding, maybe £200 a month, to have three months by 2030. And I'd make myself do one proper course on the new AI systems around 2029, because by then I'd see that I had no choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. A bit like a test date you know is coming and keep putting off revising for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do a course around 2029. Why wait so long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want to see which systems actually stick. My dad bought a video recorder the year DVDs came out, and we laughed about it for years. I'd rather be late and right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this picture change anything about your plans with Hina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still marry next August, but smaller. And we'd hold off buying a house until we see what 2031 does, which Hina won't like, because she's had her eye on a cottage by the river.

Mood stays anxious: his **post** could still go, though he has some control.

steps.text: Finish family medicine training at Fernvale by 2029
Save £200 a month after the wedding

Hold off buying the riverside cottage until after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for sensible people to make sensible plans. I'd say it at the surgery and to friends, and I'd mean it. There's no need to rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right for most of it. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, an experienced family doctor, maybe a partner at Fernvale if Dr Lowe retires. The hands-on work goes on until 2039, so I'd have time, but I know I'd have to learn the computer side eventually, and I'll hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and focus on getting good at medicine for the first few years. I'd save steadily and aim to buy the cottage by the river with Hina around 2029. And I'd wait until about 2032 to learn the AI systems properly, when they're settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier. Not completely relaxed, because I know it's coming, but it feels like something I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'll wait. What if waiting turns out to be the mistake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's my mistake, and I'll own it. But I've seen too many shiny things come and go in this surgery. The fax machine is still in the corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you most in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper training, during work hours, not on my days off. And somebody explaining it slowly, without making me feel stupid.

steps.text: Keep getting better at clinical medicine at Fernvale
Save to buy the riverside cottage with Hina around 2029
Wait until about 2032 before learning the AI systems

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Hina and I would both be at risk just as we're starting out, with no savings. What would help is some guarantee that young doctors aren't the first to go, and training in work hours, explained slowly. And maybe some help for couples like us so we don't lose the wedding money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the farmers. Half of them don't have proper internet up the valley. If everything moves onto apps and computers, the people who most need a doctor won't be able to reach one.

He is **pragmatic** and calm in tone, preferring to wait and follow careful colleagues.
He moves from uneasy to **alarmed** with AGI in two years, then back to uneasy with ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both his and Hina's jobs at risk and no savings.
